common_name: Purple Diamond Loropetalum (Compact Deep-Purple Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Diamond holds its rich purple foliage color best in full sun, and its naturally compact, dense habit needs little pruning to stay tidy.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water regularly the first season to establish before easing into a lower-maintenance routine. Purple Diamond is part of the First Editions breeding program and stands out among Loropetalum chinense cultivars for its unusually dense, rounded, naturally compact habit and consistently deep, dark purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season rather than fading to green, punctuated by frilly magenta-pink flowers in spring with scattered rebloom into fall. Its tidy, slow-to-medium growth rate makes it lower-maintenance than larger loropetalum cultivars, suiting foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders without frequent shearing. Prune lightly right after the spring flower flush if shaping is needed, since later pruning removes next year's flower buds.
sources: First Editions Shrubs & Trees — Purple Diamond variety notes

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; like other distylium cultivars, Coppertone is remarkably adaptable to both wet and dry sites and to sun or shade once established.

directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it as a low-maintenance evergreen hedge, foundation shrub, or mass planting where deer pressure is a concern, since distylium is rarely browsed. Coppertone is a First Editions selection of distylium prized for its striking bronze-copper new growth in spring, which matures to glossy dark green, giving the shrub a two-toned seasonal display on a mounding, medium-sized evergreen frame, with small maroon-red flowers appearing inconspicuously along the stems in late winter. It shares the exceptional adaptability of the species — thriving in full sun or full shade, wet or dry soil, and resisting the leaf spot and scale problems that trouble many broadleaf evergreens in humid Gulf South summers. Requires only occasional shaping, as its naturally dense, mounded form rarely needs hard pruning.
sources: First Editions Shrubs & Trees — Coppertone variety notes

common_name: Blue Cascade Distylium (Spreading Groundcover Evergreen Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Blue Cascade spreads wider than it grows tall, making it useful as a large-scale evergreen groundcover on slopes or under high tree canopy where mowing is impractical.

directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, spacing plants to allow the low, wide-spreading branches to knit together into a dense evergreen groundcover over a couple of seasons. Blue Cascade is a low, mounding, ground-hugging distylium selection with fine-textured, blue-green foliage that cascades over walls, banks, and slopes, sharing the parent species' resistance to leaf spot, scale, and deer browsing along with tolerance for both wet and dry, sunny and shaded sites. Its width-over-height habit makes it a durable substitute for juniper or low spreading yew in Gulf South landscapes, where those traditional groundcover shrubs often struggle with heat, humidity, and root rot. Requires little to no pruning beyond removing an occasional wayward branch to keep the mounded outline tidy.
sources: First Editions Shrubs & Trees — Blue Cascade variety notes

common_name: April Dawn Camellia (Cold-Hardy Variegated Ackerman Hybrid Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; April Dawn was bred for cold hardiness and blooms later than most japonica camellias, avoiding much of the flower bud damage from late-winter freezes common in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5–6.0) in partial shade, and mulch well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Bred by Dr. William Ackerman at the U.S. National Arboretum as part of his cold-hardy camellia breeding program crossing Camellia japonica with the hardier C. oleifera, April Dawn produces large, formal double blooms of white heavily streaked and marbled with pink, opening in late winter to early spring on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its late bloom timing and improved cold hardiness compared to standard japonica camellias make it more reliable in the northern Gulf South and in years with a late hard freeze, since fewer flower buds are lost to cold damage. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape, and avoid heavy pruning in fall, which removes the developing flower buds.
sources: U.S. National Arboretum — Ackerman camellia breeding program
